extracted.intended_audience: citizens and voters of New York; the general public interested in the Constitution and design of the federal government
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative exposition assessing whether and how the national government should be empowered to regulate the times, places, and manner of elections for federal offices, and related principles about representation and assembly size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-preservation principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Every government ought to contain in itself the means of its own preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions should reserve discretionary powers necessary for their own survival; it is impractical to attempt to fix every future election law in the text of the Constitution because circumstances change, so some authority to interpose for security must be lodged somewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservation to states with national override
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation of elections for the federal government submitted in the first instance to the local administrations, but the national authority reserved a right to interpose whenever extraordinary circumstances render that interposition necessary to its safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The convention's compromise: let states handle ordinary election regulation for convenience and satisfaction, but give Congress power to alter time, place, and manner in exceptional cases as a constitutional safeguard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of exclusive state control over federal elections
rubrics_metrics.description: An exclusive power of regulating elections for the national government in the hands of the State legislatures would leave the existence of the Union entirely at their mercy; they could at any moment annihilate it by neglecting to provide for the choice of persons to administer its affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not trust national survival solely to state legislatures; the constitutional possibility of neglect or malicious inaction is an unanswerable objection to exclusive state control. The risk cannot be justified by speculative assurances that it would not occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate composition mitigates risk (tenure and rotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because senators have six-year terms, rotation by thirds, a two-senators-per-state rule, and a small quorum (sixteen), a temporary combination of a few States could neither annul the existence nor impair the activity of the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design features (longer terms, staggered turnover, small per-state representation) make the Senate less vulnerable to short-term conspiracies among state legislatures, lessening the danger associated with state influence over some federal appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: House frequent elections increase vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Representatives is to have general elections once in two years: if State legislatures had exclusive authority over the regulation of these elections, every election period would be a delicate crisis which might issue in a dissolution of the Union if a few leading States conspired to prevent an election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent turnover in a legislative body heightens the risk that concerted action by a few state governments could interrupt representation and threaten the continuity of the national government; thus some federal authority over election regulation is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence between popular interest and state rulers' interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The interest of the people in the public felicity may differ from the interest of their local rulers in the power and consequence of their offices; local rulers, stimulated by rivalry, hopes of personal aggrandizement, or factional support, may act contrary to the people's attachment to the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because state leaders can have motives (personal advancement, faction) that diverge from the public good, relying solely on state legislatures to secure national elections is inadequate; this risk supports a federal backstop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on national regulation: times, places, and manner only; qualifications immutable
rubrics_metrics.description: The national authority would be expressly restricted to the regulation of the TIMES, the PLACES, the MANNER of elections; the qualifications of those who may choose or be chosen are defined in the Constitution and unalterable by the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress's power over elections is deliberately narrow—procedural, not substantive; it cannot change constitutional qualification requirements (e.g., property, age, citizenship) and therefore cannot effect certain forms of disenfranchisement by indirect expedients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improbability of national bias due to structural diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissimilarity in the ingredients and modes of constituting the various branches (House elected directly, Senate by state legislatures, President by electors) and the variety of local interests make it unlikely the national government would concert a scheme to prefer a particular class of citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural checks and the heterogeneous composition of national institutions (different selection methods and varied regional interests) act as safeguards against the national government adopting partial election regulations to favor a particular economic or social class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits to national abuse: popular resistance and costs of force
rubrics_metrics.description: If the national rulers attempted to restrict elections to favor a class, they would almost certainly provoke an immediate revolt of the people and the State governments; to carry such a plan into effect would likely require military force and thus a bolder, more decisive usurpation than fabricating election laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical political constraints — popular sentiment, state reaction, and the high cost and visibility of using force — make certain theoretical abuses (e.g., manipulating places of election to exclude voters) implausible as stable policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: No effective method of preferring 'the wealthy and the well-born' by regulating times/places/manner
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no method of securing to the rich the preference apprehended, but by prescribing qualifications of property either for those who may elect or be elected; such qualifications do not form part of the time/place/manner power to be conferred upon the national government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fears that Congress could use procedural rules to elevate a social class are misplaced because property or other qualifications are constitutionally fixed and cannot be altered by mere regulation of election logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of inconvenient polling locations on suffrage
rubrics_metrics.description: When the place of election is at an inconvenient distance from the elector, the effect upon his conduct will be the same whether that distance be twenty miles or twenty thousand miles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical examples (e.g., appointing a single city as the election place) show that inconvenient polling locations reduce participation; this effect applies equally under state and federal authority, so the form of the power, not its holder, determines this risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal size of representative assemblies (tradeoff)
rubrics_metrics.description: After securing a sufficient number for the purposes of safety, of local information, and of diffusive sympathy with the whole society, additional representatives counteract the people's views: the more numerous an assembly, the greater the ascendency of passion over reason, and the larger the proportion of members of limited information and weak capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a tradeoff in assembly size: too few risks oligarchic control by articulate elites; too many increases susceptibility to demagogy and the influence of a few cunning speakers. Design should aim for a sufficient number for representation and information, but no more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule principle vs. supermajority/quorum requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring more than a majority for a quorum, or more than a majority of a quorum for decisions, would reverse the fundamental principle of free government: the majority would no longer rule and power would be transferred to the minority, enabling minorities to extort indulgences or facilitate secessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While higher thresholds might protect particular interests or slow hasty measures, they impose serious costs: they empower minorities to obstruct and may foster secessionist or obstructionist practices; thus default majority rule is preferred except where compelling reasons exist.
